cards.text: Psalm 17 is a prayer of David, and he goes straight to the LORD. No small talk, no "Hey, how's Your week going?" He opens with this: "Hear, O LORD, my righteous plea; listen to my cry."

cards.question: David asks the LORD to give ear to his prayer. Where does he say that prayer comes from?

cards.text: Then David says, "May my vindication come from Your presence; may Your eyes see what is right." Not the neighbors, not the comment section, not the guy at work with OPINIONS. David wants the LORD's eyes on this one.

cards.question: David says the LORD has tried his heart and even visited him in the night. When God tested him, what did He find?
David says he has made up his mind not to sin with his mouth.

cards.text: David says that by the word of God's lips, he has avoided the ways of the violent. That's a man who sees trouble coming and crosses the street. Then crosses it AGAIN, just to be safe.

cards.question: David says his steps have held to God's paths, but his feet have slipped.

cards.text: Feet that never slipped, while I'm attached to a gold base and I STILL wobble. Now David calls on God again, and he sounds completely sure of something.

cards.question: David calls on God because he's sure God will ___ him.

cards.text: David says, "Incline Your ear to me; hear my words." Then he asks God to show the wonders of His loving devotion.

cards.question: David says God saves people by His right hand. Which people?

answers.text: Those who seek refuge from their foes
Those who have never once stumbled
Those who bring the biggest offerings

cards.text: Then David paints two pictures: "Keep me as the apple of Your eye; hide me in the shadow of Your wings". Friend, that is NOT a man asking for a little personal space.

cards.question: David asks God to hide him in the shadow of His wings. Hide him from whom?

cards.text: David says these enemies have closed their callous hearts. Door shut, porch light off, and they're pretending nobody's home.

cards.question: David says his enemies speak with humility.

cards.text: And they don't just talk. David says they've tracked down him and the people with him, and now they surround them, like a bill collector who found your new number AND your new address.

cards.question: The enemies have David and the people with him surrounded. What are the enemies' eyes set on doing?

answers.text: Driving them out of the land

cards.question: David says his enemies are like a young ___ lurking in ___.

cards.text: So David cries out, "Arise, O LORD, confront them!" When there's a lion lurking, you don't text a friend. You call on the LORD.

cards.question: David asks the LORD to bring his enemies to their knees. How does he ask God to deliver him from the wicked?

cards.text: David calls them men of the world whose portion is in this life. Then he turns his prayer toward God's treasured ones.

cards.question: David asks God to fill the bellies of His treasured ones.
David keeps praying for God's treasured ones and their sons. What does he say gets left to the children?

cards.text: Then David turns the spotlight on himself: "As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness". Friend, that's a man who knows EXACTLY what he wants out of this life.

cards.question: David says that when he wakes up, he'll be ___ in God's presence.

findings.problem: The story card has 3 sentences: the quote of verse 2, "Not the neighbors, not the comment section, not the guy at work with OPINIONS." and "David wants the LORD's eyes on this one." Only the opening card can have 3 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The story card has 3 sentences: the retelling of verse 4, "That's a man who sees trouble coming and crosses the street." and "Then crosses it AGAIN, just to be safe."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: "Feet that never slipped" stretches the text. Verse 5 says "my feet have not slipped," which is not the same as never having slipped.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The wrong answers "ignore" and "forget" aren't believable. Nobody calls on God because they're sure He will ignore or forget them. The setup card even says David "sounds completely sure," so the right answer stands out and these choices read as silly.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The story card is a plain retelling of verses 6 and 7 with none of Papa Dorin's voice.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess the wording of verse 12's simile: "young ___ lurking in ___" with lion, wolf, ambush, daylight and silence. No earlier card sets up a lion or any hunting picture, so lion versus wolf is pure luck. The first simile in the verse, "like a lion greedy for prey," is never told. "daylight" is also a silly choice.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This choice card follows another choice card, but no story card gives context the baker can reason from, so the right answer depends on luck.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The story card has 3 sentences: the quote of verse 13, "When there's a lion lurking, you don't text a friend." and "You call on the LORD."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess a detail: sword, flood or fire from heaven. Nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker reason toward a sword. This matches the bad Psalm 23 example of guessing a detail.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The story card is a plain retelling of verse 14 with none of Papa Dorin's voice.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: "that's a man who knows EXACTLY what he wants out of this life" goes against the text. Verse 14 describes the men of the world as those "whose portion is in this life," and verse 15 sets David's hope apart from theirs: beholding God's face. Saying David wants something "out of this life" blurs the contrast the psalm draws.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.
